counterexample: The final deduction drops a case. From f <= 4 and f = (p-1)/2 with p > 3 prime, f = 3 gives p = 7 (and f = 4 gives p = 9, non-prime), so the surviving cases are p = 5 AND p = 7, not p = 5 alone. Concretely, for p = 7 the reduced equation is xi^3 - zeta^3 = 2^sigma with n = 3 <= P + 1 = 4, so the quoted Bugeaud-Gyory bound (P = max{2,3} = 3) does not exclude it; the case y = 14 is therefore left unresolved by the argument as written. (Ruling p = 7 out is possible - xi^3 - zeta^3 = (xi - zeta)(xi^2 + xi*zeta + zeta^2) with xi, zeta both odd forces the odd factor xi^2 + xi*zeta + zeta^2 = 1, impossible for xi > zeta > 0 - but the proof gives no such argument.)

The first two conclusions are fine - p | xi^f + zeta^f, and xi^f - zeta^f divides 2^tau so equals 2^sigma with sigma <= tau (sigma > 0 also holds, since xi,zeta must both be odd, though the proof does not say why). Applying the quoted theorem to xi^f - zeta^f = 2^sigma gives, for f >= 3, f <= max{2,3} + 1 = 4, so the theorem leaves f in {2,3,4}. With f = (p-1)/2 and p > 3 prime this leaves p = 5 (f = 2) and p = 7 (f = 3); f = 4 gives the non-prime 9. The final assertion that only p = 5 remains therefore silently discards the surviving case p = 7 (y = 14), and no argument is given against it. Since a step fails, the proof as written is invalid (and in any case it terminates with the residual case(s) unresolved rather than establishing the claimed non-existence).
